headline: White Island Ledge Gives Up Haddock to 6, Bluefish Finally Crash Rye Harbor
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which six feet of it hold fish — this week it was the Shoals ledges and a sudden bluefish push at Rye Harbor.
body_markdown:
People from away always ask me how I fish the same thirteen miles of coast every week without getting bored. I tell them the same thing every time: New Hampshire doesn't have thirteen miles of coastline, it has thirteen miles of front door and about a hundred and thirty miles of water once you count the Shoals, the ledges, the river mouth, and every piece of structure in between. You just have to fish it like you mean it. This week meant leaving Rye Harbor before 5 a.m. with the Lund loaded light, because the haddock have been up on the humps around White Island and Duck Island, and if you're not anchored up or drifting the top of that structure by first light, you're fishing leftovers.

The groundfish bite out at the Shoals has been honest, not spectacular. White Island Ledge in 60 to 80 feet gave up haddock to six pounds on the last two mornings I ran out, mixed with a few keeper cod pushing seven and eight, all on the bottom of the tide when the current eases enough to hold a jig vertical. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid have been outfishing bare metal — the fish are picky enough right now that they want a little scent riding down with the flash. Once the tide starts to run hard past half-flood or half-ebb, that bite shuts off fast. You get maybe a ninety-minute window on each side of the slack, and if you're not rigged and dropped when it opens, you watch it close. I've had mornings out there where three of us put a dozen fish in the box in that window and then sat on a stone-cold rip for two hours waiting for the next one. That's the Shoals in July — you fish the clock, not the location.

Mackerel have finally shown in numbers around Appledore and the backside of Star Island, which matters more than people think, because that's the bait that's been pulling bigger cod up off bottom to chase. If you see the birds working tight over showers of mackerel near the ledges, drop a sabiki first, then switch over to a bigger jig once you've got a few mackerel in the well — a live mack fished on a heavy jig head near bottom has out-produced anything artificial out there this week.

Inshore, the striper story is Hampton Harbor, and it's been better than the ocean side has any right to expect given how warm and quiet the surf's been. Fish are stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming, pushing bait up through the inlet channel and holding along the edges where the current breaks against the jetty rocks. I've seen slot bass to 32 inches taken on white paddletails fished slow along that seam, and live pogies under a slip float have been money for the guys willing to soak bait instead of cast all day. The key has been fishing that inlet on the push, not the drain — on the outgoing the current rips too hard and flattens out the structure the fish are using. Give it that two-hour incoming window around the new tide change and work the drop-off just inside the jetty tips.

Bluefish showed up harder than I expected this week, cutting through Rye Harbor and pushing bait right up against the rocks at Odiorne Point. These aren't the giant choppers yet, mostly two to four pounds, but they're aggressive and they've been busting bait on top in the mornings, which makes for the kind of visual bite that gets people using words like exciting instead of technical. Topwater poppers and single-hook Kastmasters have worked, but bring wire or heavy fluoro leader — I lost three good lures in two days before I remembered who I was dealing with.

Flounder in the Piscataqua and up into Portsmouth Harbor have been a mixed bag — some days you can put together a dozen keepers drifting the deeper holes off the Route 1 bridge on the last of the ebb, other days you soak clams and worms for two hours and get nothing but hermit crabs. The river's still cold enough on bottom to hold fish, but the bite's been tide-dependent to the point where I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now. Better to treat it as a bonus stop on the way back in from the Shoals.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd keep working that White Island slack window early and expect the mackerel push to keep building, which should hold the bigger cod up shallower through the week. In the harbor, I'd fish that incoming tide hard at Hampton for another week or two before the bass start sliding out toward the open coast as the water warms further. And if you see bluefish showing at Odiorne again on a calm morning, don't wait — that bite's been unpredictable, on some days and gone the next, and I'd rather catch it than chase it.
